implementation_notes: Python expresses the deferral with descriptors instead of a validator object: a @property recomputes the check on each access and functools.cached_property (3.8+) runs it once and stores the result in the instance dictionary, which replaces the classic Validator class for the common case. Dataclasses and attrs validate in __post_init__ or through field validators at construction - the eager opposite - so use them for values that must always be valid and the cached property for objects assembled over time and checked per use. A hand-written validate_for_publish() returning a list of violations is still the right shape when the caller needs the whole error set rather than the first exception.
pitfalls: functools.cached_property needs an instance __dict__: with __slots__ and no __dict__ slot, or with a frozen dataclass, the failure is an AttributeError at first use rather than at class definition.
The cached verdict goes stale after mutation, because the underlying state changed while publish_errors kept the old list; invalidate explicitly or use a plain @property and accept recomputation.

Any read triggers the check, including introspection - hasattr probes, a dataclass repr, a debugger - so a validation that raises inside a property can break code that never intended to use the value.
